uses: In Ayurveda, the traditional medicine of India, tulsi is honored as the queen of herbs and has long been used for fevers, coughs and asthma, indigestion and stiff joints. It is also a sacred plant in Hinduism: many households keep one in a pot in the courtyard, tend it in morning and evening rituals, and take its leaves or a tulsi tea as part of daily devotion. Today it is often drunk as a calming tea and sold as an adaptogen, an herb said to help the body cope with stress.
taste: Hot and bitter, with a spicy note of clove and mint
energetics: Ayurveda describes tulsi as drying and penetrating, balancing kapha and vata
caution_pregnancy: Holy basil might not be safe if you are pregnant or trying to conceive: in animal studies, large amounts made it harder for a fertilized egg to implant and for pregnancy to go to term. Whether this happens in people isn't known, so avoid it while trying to conceive and during pregnancy. Safety while breastfeeding hasn't been studied; avoid.
caution_medications: It may slow blood clotting, so take care with blood thinners and anti-platelet drugs, including aspirin. It may make thyroid hormone medicine less effective. Animal data suggest it can deepen the sedation from barbiturates. Small studies found it lowered blood sugar, including alongside a diabetes drug, so if you take diabetes medicines ask your prescriber and watch for lows.
caution_conditions: It may lower thyroxine levels and worsen an underactive thyroid. It may raise the risk of bleeding during and after surgery, so tell your surgeon you take it. Side effects can include nausea, diarrhea, headache and feeling agitated. Holy basil is a different plant from the sweet basil used in cooking.
caution_duration: Holy basil seems safe for most people for up to 8 weeks by mouth; longer use hasn't been studied.
caution_topical: Our sources don't cover putting holy basil on the skin, so not enough is known about skin use.
garden_water: Moist but well-drained soil; does poorly when waterlogged
notes: A tender, bushy annual or short-lived perennial from tropical southern Asia, growing quickly to about 3 feet and self-sowing freely; keep it in a container or a confined bed, as it can turn weedy outside its native range. Japanese beetles may strip the leaves; pick them off by hand. Its clove-like scent comes from eugenol and is said to keep insects away. Culpeper and Grieve describe only sweet basil, so no planet is given.
